title: Cranial Nerve V (The Trigeminal Nerve)
subtitle: Sorting facial numbness, pain and jaw weakness into supranuclear, nuclear, root, ganglion and peripheral-branch lesions

points.text: Supranuclear control comes from the lower precentral gyrus.
points.quote: It receives its supranuclear control through corticobulbar fibers originating in the lower third of the precentral gyrus.

points.text: The bilateral corticobulbar connections descend through the corona radiata, internal capsule and peduncle and cross in the pons before reaching the motor nuclei.
points.quote: These bilateral connections travel through the corona radiata, internal capsule, and cerebral peduncle and decussate in the pons before supplying the motor nuclei.

points.text: The motor root leaves the skull with V3 through the foramen ovale and joins it to form the mandibular nerve, which supplies the masticatory muscles.
points.quote: After leaving the skull, the motor root joins the mandibular (third) division of the trigeminal nerve to form the mandibular nerve

points.text: The spinal nucleus carries pain, temperature and soft touch from the face and mucous membranes.
points.quote: receives fibers that convey the sensations of pain, temperature, and soft touch from the face and mucous membranes

points.text: The main sensory nucleus, in the lateral pons, serves tactile and proprioceptive sensation.
points.quote: Fibers entering this nucleus are concerned with tactile and proprioceptive sensation.

points.text: The mesencephalic nucleus receives proprioception from the masticatory muscles and from muscles of other motor cranial nerves.
points.quote: This nucleus receives proprioceptive impulses from the masticatory muscles and from muscles supplied by other motor cranial nerves.

points.text: Ophthalmic fibers lie ventral in the spinal tract and reach the lowest levels; mandibular fibers lie dorsal and end most rostrally.
points.quote: The fibers of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve travel in the most ventral part of the spinal tract

points.text: The rostral-caudal arrangement of the spinal nucleus (perioral rostral, lateral face caudal) underlies the onionskin pattern.
points.quote: This onionskin segmental distribution reflects the rostral-caudal somatotopy of the cutaneous distribution of the spinal nucleus

points.text: V1 runs in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus beside CN III, IV and VI and enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure.
points.quote: lies in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus in close association with the third, fourth, and sixth cranial nerves

points.text: V2 passes through the inferolateral cavernous sinus and exits via the foramen rotundum.
points.quote: through the inferolateral portion of the cavernous sinus and then leaves the skull through the foramen rotundum

points.text: V3 exits through the foramen ovale into the infratemporal fossa.
points.quote: This nerve leaves the skull through the foramen ovale and travels in the infratemporal fossa

points.text: The lingual branch carries general sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue; taste travels with the facial nerve.
points.quote: the anterior two-thirds of the tongue (not taste sensation, which is carried by the facial nerve)

localizationRules.explanation: A lesion distal to the gasserian ganglion affects one division's skin territory; a lesion at or proximal to the ganglion affects the whole ipsilateral face.
localizationRules.quote: Lesions of individual divisions (distal to the gasserian ganglion) result in sensory loss confined to the cutaneous supply of that division

localizationRules.explanation: Pain/temperature loss with preserved touch points to the spinal tract and nucleus rather than the main sensory nucleus.
localizationRules.quote: differentiates lesions affecting the spinal tract and nucleus of the trigeminal nerve from lesions affecting the main sensory nucleus

localizationRules.rule: Jaw deviation with nuclear or infranuclear lesions
localizationRules.explanation: With a motor nucleus or peripheral motor lesion the jaw deviates toward the weak side on opening, because the opposite lateral pterygoid acts unopposed.
localizationRules.quote: the jaw deviates to the paralyzed side when the mouth is opened (due to contraction of the contralateral intact lateral pterygoid muscle)

localizationRules.explanation: Cortical control is bilateral with a contralateral predominance for the masseter, so unilateral lesions give mild weakness; bilateral upper motor neuron lesions give marked weakness.
localizationRules.quote: Supranuclear control of trigeminal motor function is bilateral; however, the contralateral hemisphere exerts predominant control on the voluntary activity of the masseter

localizationRules.explanation: The afferent limb is V1 and the efferent limb is the facial nerve on both sides, so a trigeminal lesion abolishes both the direct and the consensual response.
localizationRules.quote: Lesions of the trigeminal nerve result in loss of the ipsilateral and contralateral responses.

keySyndromes.name: Wallenberg syndrome (trigeminal component)
keySyndromes.triad: Loss of pain and temperature over the ipsilateral face + often contralateral body and limb sensory loss + spinal trigeminal nucleus involvement
keySyndromes.clue: The spinal nucleus is characteristically affected; the typical pattern is loss over the whole side of the face.
keySyndromes.quote: In the typical syndrome, pain and temperature sensation are lost over the entire side of the face.

keySyndromes.name: Cerebellopontine angle extension
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral facial pain, paresthesias and sensory loss + masticatory paresis + depressed corneal reflex + ipsilateral tinnitus, deafness and vertigo
keySyndromes.clue: Usually vestibular schwannoma or meningioma; cranial nerve VIII involvement distinguishes it from a pure trigeminal lesion.
keySyndromes.quote: Ipsilateral facial pain, paresthesias, sensory loss, masticatory paresis, and a depressed corneal reflex are then associated with ipsilateral tinnitus, deafness, and vertigo

keySyndromes.name: Trigeminal neuralgia
keySyndromes.triad: Sudden lancinating unilateral pain in one or more divisions + brief paroxysms + triggers from non-nociceptive facial stimulation
keySyndromes.clue: V2 is the most frequent territory, then V3 and V1; many cases are due to vascular compression or irritation of the root entry zone.
keySyndromes.quote: The painful paroxysms are often triggered by non-nociceptive facial stimulation and are often associated with facial contortions.

keySyndromes.name: Raeder paratrigeminal syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral miosis and ptosis without facial anhidrosis + ipsilateral trigeminal involvement (+ possible CN IV and VI involvement)
keySyndromes.clue: Usually a middle cranial fossa lesion between the trigeminal ganglion and the internal carotid artery near the petrous apex.
keySyndromes.quote: This uncommon syndrome is composed of two essential components: unilateral oculosympathetic paresis and evidence of trigeminal involvement on the same side

keySyndromes.name: Gradenigo syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral pain and sensory disturbance in V1 + ipsilateral lateral rectus palsy (+ oculosympathetic paresis without anhidrosis)
keySyndromes.clue: A lesion at the petrous apex affects V1 and the abducens nerve.
keySyndromes.quote: Pain and sensory disturbance in the upper part of the face (ophthalmic distribution) are then associated with ipsilateral lateral rectus palsy

keySyndromes.name: Cavernous sinus syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Ophthalmoplegia + pain, paresthesias and sensory loss in V1 (less often V2) + occasional oculosympathetic paresis
keySyndromes.clue: V3 is spared, so there is no masticatory weakness.
keySyndromes.quote: Because the mandibular nerve is spared, no masticatory paresis is evident.

boardTraps.text: The angle of the jaw is supplied by cervical roots (C2-C3), not by V; hemifacial loss that spares it favors an organic lesion.
boardTraps.quote: and not by the trigeminal nerve. Therefore, a hemifacial sensory loss that spares the angle of the jaw is probably organic

boardTraps.text: In Wallenberg syndrome the textbook dissociated trigeminal pattern was actually uncommon in one series of 50 patients; onionskin patterns were more often seen than divisional ones.
boardTraps.quote: Therefore, in this study, the so-called classic dissociated sensory pattern of lateral medullary infarction was actually uncommon

boardTraps.text: Superior orbital fissure and cavernous sinus lesions look alike clinically and usually need neuroimaging to separate them.
boardTraps.quote: the superior orbital fissure syndrome and the cavernous sinus syndrome usually cannot be differentiated clinically without the use of neuroradiologic procedures

boardTraps.text: A numb chin (mental neuropathy) without trauma should trigger a search for malignancy.
boardTraps.quote: Therefore, patients who develop a nontraumatic mental neuropathy should undergo a careful search for malignancy

boardTraps.text: Jaw-closing weakness points to myasthenia gravis, jaw-opening weakness to muscle disease, in flaccid quadriparesis.
boardTraps.quote: the presence of jaw-closing weakness pointed toward myasthenia gravis, whereas the presence of jaw-opening weakness suggested muscle disease

boardTraps.text: A mesencephalic nucleus lesion is nearly silent, at most depressing the ipsilateral jaw jerk.
boardTraps.quote: cause no apparent neurologic signs and symptoms, except perhaps depression of the ipsilateral jaw jerk
